quotes.text: "Even as a child I used to sneeze from the smoke here,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but to this day I don't understand how smoke can keep off frost."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Smoke takes the place of clouds when there are none . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And what do you want clouds for?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In overcast and cloudy weather there is no frost."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You don't say so."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Good heavens! she is grown up,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "When I went away from here last, five years ago, you were still a child. You were such a thin, longlegged creature, with your hair hanging on your shoulders; you used to wear short frocks, and I used to tease you, calling you a heron. . . . What time does!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, five years!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Much water has flowed since then. Tell me, Andryusha, honestly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "do you feel strange with us now? But why do I ask you? You are a man, you live your own interesting life, you are somebody . . . . To grow apart is so natural! But however that may be, Andryusha, I want you to think of us as your people. We have a right to that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do, Tanya."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "On your word of honour?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, on my word of honour."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You were surprised this evening that we have so many of your photographs. You know my father adores you. Sometimes it seems to me that he loves you more than he does me. He is proud of you. You are a clever, extraordinary man, you have made a brilliant career for yourself, and he is persuaded that you have turned out like this because he brought you up. I don't try to prevent him from thinking so. Let him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's time we were asleep, though,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and it's cold, too."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Thank you for coming, Andryusha. We have only uninteresting acquaintances, and not many of them. We have only the garden, the garden, the garden, and nothing else. Standards, half-standards,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Aports, Reinettes, Borovinkas, budded stocks, grafted stocks. . . . All, all our life has gone into the garden. I never even dream of anything but apples and pears. Of course, it is very nice and useful, but sometimes one longs for something else for variety. I remember that when you used to come to us for the summer holidays, or simply a visit, it always seemed to be fresher and brighter in the house, as though the covers had been taken off the lustres and the furniture. I was only a little girl then, but yet I understood it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "'Onyegin, I won't conceal it;                 I madly love Tatiana. . . .'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Here is a business, brother . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "On the surface of the ground, as you see, is frost; but if you raise the thermometer on a stick fourteen feet above the ground, there it is warm. . . . Why is that?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I really don't know,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "H'm! . . . One can't know everything, of course. . . . However large the intellect may be, you can't find room for everything in it. I suppose you still go in chiefly for philosophy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, I lecture in psychology; I am working at philosophy in general."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And it does not bore you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "On the contrary, it's all I live for."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, God bless you! . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "God bless you! . . . I am delighted about you . . . delighted, my boy. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who tied this horse to an apple-tree?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who is the low scoundrel who has dared to tie this horse to an apple-tree? My God, my God! They have ruined everything; they have spoilt everything; they have done everything filthy, horrible, and abominable. The orchard's done for, the orchard's ruined. My God!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What is one to do with these accursed people?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Styopka was carting dung at night, and tied the horse to an apple-tree! He twisted the reins round it, the rascal, as tightly as he could, so that the bark is rubbed off in three places. What do you think of that! I spoke to him and he stands like a post and only blinks his eyes. Hanging is too good for him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, God bless you! . . . God bless you! . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am very glad you have come. Unutterably glad. . . . Thank you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have been all day thinking of a legend,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I don't remember whether I have read it somewhere or heard it, but it is a strange and almost grotesque legend. To begin with, it is somewhat obscure. A thousand years ago a monk, dressed in black, wandered about the desert, somewhere in Syria or Arabia. . . . Some miles from where he was, some fisherman saw another black monk, who was moving slowly over the surface of a lake. This second monk was a mirage. Now forget all the laws of optics, which the legend does not recognise, and listen to the rest. From that mirage there was cast another mirage, then from that other a third, so that the image of the black monk began to be repeated endlessly from one layer of the atmosphere to another. So that he was seen at one time in Africa, at another in Spain, then in Italy, then in the Far North. . . . Then he passed out of the atmosphere of the earth, and now he is wandering all over the universe, still never coming into conditions in which he might disappear. Possibly he may be seen now in Mars or in some star of the Southern Cross. But, my dear, the real point on which the whole legend hangs lies in the fact that, exactly a thousand years from the day when the monk walked in the desert, the mirage will return to the atmosphere of the earth again and will appear to men. And it seems that the thousand years is almost up . . . . According to the legend, we may look out for the black monk to-day or to-morrow."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A queer mirage,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But the most wonderful part of it all,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "is that I simply cannot recall where I got this legend from. Have I read it somewhere? Have I heard it? Or perhaps I dreamed of the black monk. I swear I don't remember. But the legend interests me. I have been thinking about it all day."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How open, how free, how still it is here!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And it feels as though all the world were watching me, hiding and waiting for me to understand it. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, you see,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "there must be truth in the legend."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Here, Andryusha; read father's articles,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They are splendid articles. He writes capitally."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Capitally, indeed!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't listen to her, please; don't read them! Though, if you want to go to sleep, read them by all means; they are a fine soporific."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think they are splendid articles,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You read them, Andryusha, and persuade father to write oftener. He could write a complete manual of horticulture."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In that case, begin with Gaucher's article and these Russian articles,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "or else you won't understand. Before you read my objections, you must know what I am objecting to. But it's all nonsense . . . tiresome stuff. Besides, I believe it's bedtime."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, my boy. . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That's how it is, my dear lecturer. Here I write articles, and take part in exhibitions, and receive medals. . . . Pesotsky, they say, has apples the size of a head, and Pesotsky, they say, has made his fortune with his garden. In short, 'Kotcheby is rich and glorious.' But one asks oneself: what is it all for? The garden is certainly fine, a model. It's not really a garden, but a regular institution, which is of the greatest public importance because it marks, so to say, a new era in Russian agriculture and Russian industry. But, what's it for? What's the object of it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The fact speaks for itself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not mean in that sense. I meant to ask: what will happen to the garden when I die? In the condition in which you see it now, it would not be maintained for one month without me. The whole secret of success lies not in its being a big garden or a great number of labourers being employed in it, but in the fact that I love the work. Do you understand? I love it perhaps more than myself. Look at me; I do everything myself. I work from morning to night: I do all the grafting myself, the pruning myself, the planting myself. I do it all myself: when any one helps me I am jealous and irritable till I am rude. The whole secret lies in loving it-- that is, in the sharp eye of the master; yes, and in the master's hands, and in the feeling that makes one, when one goes anywhere for an hour's visit, sit, ill at ease, with one's heart far away, afraid that something may have happened in the garden. But when I die, who will look after it? Who will work? The gardener? The labourers? Yes? But I will tell you, my dear fellow, the worst enemy in the garden is not a hare, not a cockchafer, and not the frost, but any outside person."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And Tanya?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She can't be more harmful than a hare? She loves the work and understands it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, she loves it and understands it. If after my death the garden goes to her and she is the mistress, of course nothing better could be wished. But if, which God forbid, she should marry,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that's just it. If she marries and children come, she will have no time to think about the garden. What I fear most is: she will marry some fine gentleman, and he will be greedy, and he will let the garden to people who will run it for profit, and everything will go to the devil the very first year! In our work females are the scourge of God!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps it is egoism, but I tell you frankly: I don't want Tanya to get married. I am afraid of it! There is one young dandy comes to see us, bringing his violin and scraping on it; I know Tanya will not marry him, I know it quite well; but I can't bear to see him! Altogether, my boy, I am very queer. I know that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am very fond of you, and so I am going to speak to you openly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I deal plainly with certain delicate questions, and say exactly what I think, and I cannot endure so-called hidden thoughts. I will speak plainly: you are the only man to whom I should not be afraid to marry my daughter. You are a clever man with a good heart, and would not let my beloved work go to ruin; and the chief reason is that I love you as a son, and I am proud of you. If Tanya and you could get up a romance somehow, then-- well! I should be very glad and even happy. I tell you this plainly, without mincing matters, like an honest man."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If Tanya and you had a son, I would make a horticulturist of him,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "However, this is idle dreaming. Goodnight."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "On Intercropping"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A few Words on the Remarks of Monsieur Z. concerning the Trenching of the Soil for a New Garden"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Additional Matter concerning Grafting with a Dormant Bud"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Audiatur altera pars,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Sapienti sat"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "at the learned ignorance of our recognised horticultural authorities, who observe Nature from the height of their university chairs,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "whose success has been the work of the vulgar and the dilettanti."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And then followed an inappropriate, affected, and insincere regret that peasants who stole fruit and broke the branches could not nowadays be flogged.  It is beautiful, charming, healthy work, but even in this there is strife and passion,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I suppose that everywhere and in all careers men of ideas are nervous, and marked by exaggerated sensitiveness. Most likely it must be so."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I am all right, and I am doing no harm to any one; so there is no harm in my hallucinations,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, my God! My God!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Tanya! Tanya!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Leave me alone, if you please."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Fie, fie, for shame!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is it really so serious? Fie, fie!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But if you knew how he tortures me!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He torments me to death,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I said nothing to him . . . nothing . . . I only said that there was no need to keep . . . too many labourers . . . if we could hire them by the day when we wanted them. You know . . . you know the labourers have been doing nothing for a whole week. . . . I. . . I. . . only said that, and he shouted and . . . said . . . a lot of horrible insulting things to me. What for?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There, there,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You've quarrelled with each other, you've cried, and that's enough. You must not be angry for long-- that's wrong . . . all the more as he loves you beyond everything."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He has . . . has spoiled my whole life,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I hear nothing but abuse and . . . insults. He thinks I am of no use in the house. Well! He is right. I shall go away to-morrow; I shall become a telegraph clerk. . . . I don't care. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Come, come, come. . . . You mustn't cry, Tanya. You mustn't, dear . . . . You are both hot-tempered and irritable, and you are both to blame. Come along; I will reconcile you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But you are a mirage,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why are you here and sitting still? That does not fit in with the legend."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That does not matter,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The legend, the mirage, and I are all the products of your excited imagination. I am a phantom."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then you don't exist?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You can think as you like,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I exist in your imagination, and your imagination is part of nature, so I exist in nature."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You have a very old, wise, and extremely expressive face, as though you really had lived more than a thousand years,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I did not know that my imagination was capable of creating such phenomena. But why do you look at me with such enthusiasm? Do you like me?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, you are one of those few who are justly called the chosen of God. You do the service of eternal truth. Your thoughts, your designs, the marvellous studies you are engaged in, and all your life, bear the Divine, the heavenly stamp, seeing that they are consecrated to the rational and the beautiful-- that is, to what is eternal."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You said 'eternal truth.' . . . But is eternal truth of use to man and within his reach, if there is no eternal life?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is eternal life,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you believe in the immortality of man?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, of course. A grand, brilliant future is in store for you men. And the more there are like you on earth, the sooner will this future be realised. Without you who serve the higher principle and live in full understanding and freedom, mankind would be of little account; developing in a natural way, it would have to wait a long time for the end of its earthly history. You will lead it some thousands of years earlier into the kingdom of eternal truth-- and therein lies your supreme service. You are the incarnation of the blessing of God, which rests upon men."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And what is the object of eternal life?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "As of all life-- enjoyment. True enjoyment lies in knowledge, and eternal life provides innumerable and inexhaustible sources of knowledge, and in that sense it has been said: 'In My Father's house there are many mansions.'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If only you knew how pleasant it is to hear you!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am very glad."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I know that when you go away I shall be worried by the question of your reality. You are a phantom, an hallucination. So I am mentally deranged, not normal?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What if you are? Why trouble yourself? You are ill because you have overworked and exhausted yourself, and that means that you have sacrificed your health to the idea, and the time is near at hand when you will give up life itself to it. What could be better? That is the goal towards which all divinely endowed, noble natures strive."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If I know I am mentally affected, can I trust myself?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And are you sure that the men of genius, whom all men trust, did not see phantoms, too? The learned say now that genius is allied to madness. My friend, healthy and normal people are only the common herd. Reflections upon the neurasthenia of the age, nervous exhaustion and degeneracy, et cetera, can only seriously agitate those who place the object of life in the present-- that is, the common herd."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The Romans used to say: Mens sana in corpore sano."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not everything the Greeks and the Romans said is true. Exaltation, enthusiasm, ecstasy-- all that distinguishes prophets, poets, martyrs for the idea, from the common folk-- is repellent to the animal side of man-- that is, his physical health. I repeat, if you want to be healthy and normal, go to the common herd."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Strange that you repeat what often comes into my mind,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is as though you had seen and overheard my secret thoughts. But don't let us talk about me. What do you mean by 'eternal truth'?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The hallucination is over,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's a pity."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are you here?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And we have been looking and looking for you. . . . But what is the matter with you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How strange you are, Andryusha!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am pleased, Tanya,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am more than pleased: I am happy. Tanya, darling Tanya, you are an extraordinary, nice creature. Dear Tanya, I am so glad, I am so glad!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have just passed through an exalted, wonderful, unearthly moment. But I can't tell you all about it or you would call me mad and not believe me. Let us talk of you. Dear, delightful Tanya! I love you, and am used to loving you. To have you near me, to meet you a dozen times a day, has become a necessity of my existence; I don't know how I shall get on without you when I go back home."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "you will forget about us in two days. We are humble people and you are a great man."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No; let us talk in earnest!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I shall take you with me, Tanya. Yes? Will you come with me? Will you be mine?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Come,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I was not thinking of it . . . I was not thinking of it,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I want a love that will dominate me altogether; and that love only you, Tanya, can give me. I am happy! I am happy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How lovely she is!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Say what you like, there is a great deal in blood. His mother was a wonderful woman, most high-minded and intelligent. It was a pleasure to look at her good, candid, pure face; it was like the face of an angel. She drew splendidly, wrote verses, spoke five foreign languages, sang. . . . Poor thing! she died of consumption. The Kingdom of Heaven be hers."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "When he was a boy and growing up in my house, he had the same angelic face, good and candid. The way he looks and talks and moves is as soft and elegant as his mother's. And his intellect! We were always struck with his intelligence. To be sure, it's not for nothing he's a Master of Arts! It's not for nothing! And wait a bit, Ivan Karlovitch, what will he be in ten years' time? He will be far above us!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The devils! They have spoilt everything! They have ruined everything! They have spoilt everything! The garden's done for, the garden's ruined!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "a flourish"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Good-morning,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What are you thinking of now?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Of fame,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In the French novel I have just been reading, there is a description of a young savant, who does silly things and pines away through worrying about fame. I can't understand such anxiety."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Because you are wise. Your attitude towards fame is one of indifference, as towards a toy which no longer interests you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, that is true."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Renown does not allure you now. What is there flattering, amusing, or edifying in their carving your name on a tombstone, then time rubbing off the inscription together with the gilding? Moreover, happily there are too many of you for the weak memory of mankind to be able to retain your names."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Of course,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Besides, why should they be remembered? But let us talk of something else. Of happiness, for instance. What is happiness?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In ancient times a happy man grew at last frightened of his happiness --it was so great!-- and to propitiate the gods he brought as a sacrifice his favourite ring. Do you know, I, too, like Polykrates, begin to be uneasy of my happiness. It seems strange to me that from morning to night I feel nothing but joy; it fills my whole being and smothers all other feelings. I don't know what sadness, grief, or boredom is. Here I am not asleep; I suffer from sleeplessness, but I am not dull. I say it in earnest; I begin to feel perplexed."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But why?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is joy a supernatural feeling? Ought it not to be the normal state of man? The more highly a man is developed on the intellectual and moral side, the more independent he is, the more pleasure life gives him. Socrates, Diogenes, and Marcus Aurelius, were joyful, not sorrowful. And the Apostle tells us: 'Rejoice continually'; 'Rejoice and be glad.'"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But will the gods be suddenly wrathful?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If they take from me comfort and make me go cold and hungry, it won't be very much to my taste."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Andryusha, whom are you talking to?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Andryusha! Whom?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh! Whom?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, to him. . . . He is sitting here,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is no one here . . . no one! Andryusha, you are ill!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are ill!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Forgive me, my precious, my dear one, but I have noticed for a long time that your mind is clouded in some way. . . . You are mentally ill, Andryusha. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's nothing, Tanya; it's nothing,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I really am not quite well . . . it's time to admit that."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have noticed it for a long time . . . and father has noticed it,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You talk to yourself, smile somehow strangely . . . and can't sleep. Oh, my God, my God, save us!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But don't be frightened, Andryusha; for God's sake don't be frightened. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't be frightened, Andryusha,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "don't be frightened. . . . Father, it will all pass over . . . it will all pass over. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Congratulate me; it appears I have gone out of my mind"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I believe it is time for you to have your milk,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, it is not time yet . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Drink it yourself; I don't want it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You notice yourself that milk does you good."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, a great deal of good!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I congratulate you: I have gained a pound in weight since Friday."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, why have you cured me? Preparations of bromide, idleness, hot baths, supervision, cowardly consternation at every mouthful, at every step-- all this will reduce me at last to idiocy. I went out of my mind, I had megalomania; but then I was cheerful, confident, and even happy; I was interesting and original. Now I have become more sensible and stolid, but I am just like every one else: I am-- mediocrity; I am weary of life. . . . Oh, how cruelly you have treated me! . . . I saw hallucinations, but what harm did that do to any one? I ask, what harm did that do any one?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Goodness knows what you are saying!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It's positively wearisome to listen to it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then don't listen."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How fortunate Buddha, Mahomed, and Shakespeare were that their kind relations and doctors did not cure them of their ecstasy and their inspiration,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If Mahomed had taken bromide for his nerves, had worked only two hours out of the twenty-four, and had drunk milk, that remarkable man would have left no more trace after him than his dog. Doctors and kind relations will succeed in stupefying mankind, in making mediocrity pass for genius and in bringing civilisation to ruin. If only you knew,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "how grateful I am to you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Father adores you. You are cross with him about something, and it is killing him. Look at him; he is ageing, not from day to day, but from hour to hour. I entreat you, Andryusha, for God's sake, for the sake of your dead father, for the sake of my peace of mind, be affectionate to him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I can't, I don't want to."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But why?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Explain why."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Because he is antipathetic to me, that's all,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But we won't talk about him: he is your father."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I can't understand, I can't,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Something incomprehensible, awful, is going on in the house. You have changed, grown unlike yourself. . . . You, clever, extraordinary man as you are, are irritated over trifles, meddle in paltry nonsense. . . . Such trivial things excite you, that sometimes one is simply amazed and can't believe that it is you. Come, come, don't be angry, don't be angry,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are clever, kind, noble. You will be just to father. He is so good."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is not good; he is just good-natured. Burlesque old uncles like your father, with well-fed, good-natured faces, extraordinarily hospitable and queer, at one time used to touch me and amuse me in novels and in farces and in life; now I dislike them. They are egoists to the marrow of their bones. What disgusts me most of all is their being so well-fed, and that purely bovine, purely hoggish optimism of a full stomach."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "This is torture,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not one moment of peace since the winter. . . . Why, it's awful! My God! I am wretched."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh, of course, I am Herod, and you and your father are the innocents. Of course."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My father is just dead. I owe that to you, for you have killed him. Our garden is being ruined; strangers are managing it already --that is, the very thing is happening that poor father dreaded. That, too, I owe to you. I hate you with my whole soul, and I hope you may soon perish. Oh, how wretched I am! Insufferable anguish is burning my soul. . . . My curses on you. I took you for an extraordinary man, a genius; I loved you, and you have turned out a madman. . . ."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why did you not believe me?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If you had believed me then, that you were a genius, you would not have spent these two years so gloomily and so wretchedly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Tanya!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Tanya!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown
